# Part 6: Coefficient Standard Error

## Aim

The aim is to estimate the standard error of one coefficient from the final Part 2 regression (Model 2) with the **bootstrap**, and to compare it with the standard error reported by `lm()`. I chose the coefficient for **maximum wind speed** (`wind_speed_10m_max`), because it is not part of the interaction term, so it has a single simple interpretation: the change in maximum temperature per extra km/h of wind.

## Bootstrap standard error

The bootstrap draws 2000 new data sets of the same size by sampling days **with replacement** from the original data, refits Model 2 to each, and records the wind coefficient. The standard deviation of those 2000 coefficients is the bootstrap standard error.

```{r boot}
set.seed(2026)
B <- 2000
coef_name <- "wind_speed_10m_max"

# Standard bootstrap: resample individual days with replacement
boot_iid <- replicate(B, {
  i <- sample(n, n, replace = TRUE)
  coef(lm(formula(m2), data = weather[i, ]))[coef_name]
})

# Block bootstrap: resample blocks of 30 consecutive days, to respect the
# day-to-day dependence found in Part 2 (autocorrelation of residuals)
L <- 30
n_blocks <- ceiling(n / L)
boot_block <- replicate(B, {
  starts <- sample(1:(n - L + 1), n_blocks, replace = TRUE)
  i <- unlist(lapply(starts, function(s) s:(s + L - 1)))[1:n]
  coef(lm(formula(m2), data = weather[i, ]))[coef_name]
})

# Compare the three standard errors and 95% percentile intervals
se_lm <- summary(m2)$coefficients[coef_name, "Std. Error"]
comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = c("lm() formula", "Bootstrap (resample days)", "Block bootstrap (30-day blocks)"),
  Estimate = coef(m2)[coef_name],
  Std_Error = c(se_lm, sd(boot_iid), sd(boot_block)),
  CI_lower = c(confint(m2)[coef_name, 1], quantile(boot_iid, 0.025), quantile(boot_block, 0.025)),
  CI_upper = c(confint(m2)[coef_name, 2], quantile(boot_iid, 0.975), quantile(boot_block, 0.975)),
  row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4, caption = "Standard error of the wind speed coefficient")

# Histogram of the bootstrap coefficients
hist(boot_iid, breaks = 40, main = "Bootstrap distribution of the wind speed coefficient",
     xlab = "Coefficient (degrees C per km/h)")
abline(v = coef(m2)[coef_name], col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

**Interpretation.** The `lm()` standard error is `r round(se_lm, 4)`, and the standard bootstrap gives `r round(sd(boot_iid), 4)`, which is `r round(100 * (sd(boot_iid) / se_lm - 1))`% larger. The two are close, which supports using the `lm()` formulas for this coefficient, but the bootstrap is a little bigger. This is consistent with the Part 2 diagnostics, where the residuals had unequal variance and heavy tails. `lm()` assumes constant variance and normal errors, and the bootstrap does not. The block bootstrap gives a larger standard error again (`r round(sd(boot_block), 4)`, `r round(100 * (sd(boot_block) / se_lm - 1))`% above `lm()`), because it keeps the day-to-day dependence in the data. This is what the lag-1 residual correlation of 0.27 in Part 2 suggested: the `lm()` standard errors are slightly too small because neighbouring days are not independent. Even so, the 95% interval from the block bootstrap (`r round(quantile(boot_block, 0.025), 3)` to `r round(quantile(boot_block, 0.975), 3)`) stays below zero, so the conclusion that stronger wind goes with a cooler maximum temperature in Parramatta does not change.

## Training error against cross-validated error: overfitting

The Part 5 results show almost no gap between training and cross-validated error. For the regression the training RMSE is `r round(train_rmse, 3)` °C and the 10-fold CV RMSE is `r round(cv10_rmse, 3)` °C, a difference of `r round(cv10_rmse - train_rmse, 3)` °C. For the logistic regression the training error is `r round(100 * train_err, 1)`% and the CV error is `r round(100 * cv10_err, 1)`%. Overfitting would show up as a training error that is much lower than the CV error. It is absent here because the models are simple (8 coefficients for the regression and 5 for the logistic model) and are fitted to `r nrow(weather)` days, so there is little room to fit noise. The same reasoning explains why the more flexible QDA and KNN in Part 4 did not beat the linear methods. The one sign of a gap is the stricter leave-one-year-out result (`r round(loyo_rmse, 2)` °C), which is a little worse than the random-fold estimate. That is not overfitting to noise. It reflects that individual years differ from each other, and a model trained on other years carries that extra uncertainty.

## Conclusion for Parramatta

Our models for Parramatta's weather are about as good on new days as they are on the days they were fitted to. A typical error in predicting the daily maximum temperature is about 2.5 °C, and about 18% of days are misclassified as rain or dry, with somewhat larger errors for a whole unseen year. The standard errors from `lm()` are reasonable, but the bootstrap, and especially the block bootstrap, shows they are a little optimistic because weather on consecutive days is related.

**Limitations and further analysis.** (1) Random folds ignore the time order of the data, and leave-one-year-out is based on only five years, so the estimates are not precise. (2) The block length of 30 days was chosen by judgement, and other lengths would give somewhat different standard errors. (3) Only the wind coefficient was bootstrapped, and the other coefficients could behave differently. (4) A time-series model with the previous day's weather as predictors, and a longer record of Parramatta weather, would give firmer conclusions.
